doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: Shearing plays a fugue at the Matador and lessons from him
summary: Shearing played all three parts of a written fugue flawlessly at the Matador, and Piltzecker reflects on what he learned.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: piano, the guitar and the vibes. And we all danced around each other like contrapuntal music —

Oh yeah, written out. I mean not just the blowing part, but this was before, over the chorus or something. But it went on for several choruses. Right? I studiously, I worked really hard on this thing and it was sort of cool you know. And yet, and he says this to the audience, and then he sits down and he plays all three parts flawlessly. He had never played them before. He had heard them, because we had done them on the tour, but he just goes bamm, and the entire fugue happened, right? Right there in front of my ears and I went [gestures] my jaw just — and then I realized who I’m dealing with. This is like Mozart, I mean this guy has some kind of processing power that’s really magnificent.
That’s a good way to put it, processing power.

Oh my gosh. It was amazing. And so I loved my time, I learned a lot, I wish I had been a bit more mature, I would have learned more you know. I wish I had been really ready, a more mature musician, and when I entered the quintet you know I was a little young and restless and anxious to play my four mallet stuff you know. But I learned so much about music from George, and just sensitivity and certainly you know playing in an ensemble, ensemble playing, you have to be, as I indicated. But the music got a little, you know, we played some Chick Corea, we played “Freedom Jazz Dance” and, but a lot of the stuff we did was pretty mild you know. [Scats], and I’d play these little parts and I would look at the drummer, Rusty. We’d be on stage and he would get it, his timing was so great. Just as I’d look at him he would get a nod, as if he’s falling off asleep, he’s going [gestures] and I don’t know if he knew it was going to make me laugh you know. And then we’d turn on and George would play “Conception” or something and just tear it up.
